analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set a strict drinking water standard for hexavalent chromium, a cancer-causing chemical.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA, within a year, to issue a health advisory and a national drinking water standard for hexavalent chromium (Chrome 6) that is protective of pregnant women, infants, and children. The existing federal tap water standard for total chromium dates to 1991 and does not distinguish Chrome 6, which animal studies and EPA reviews link to cancer and other harm. The bill never advanced past its first referral in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant women, infants, and children, and everyone who drinks tap water in the 31 cities where testing found Chrome 6, because they would get a health advisory and a legally binding national limit set to protect the most vulnerable.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish, within 90 days of enactment, a health advisory for hexavalent chromium that is fully protective of pregnant women, infants, and children, considering body weight, exposure patterns, and all routes of exposure.

Requires the EPA to propose within 180 days and finalize within one year a national primary drinking water regulation for hexavalent chromium, with a maximum contaminant level as close to the health goal as feasible.

The bill's findings note the existing EPA tap water standard for total chromium was set in 1991 at 100 parts per billion, while California set a public health goal for Chrome 6 of 0.02 parts per billion in 2011 — a roughly 5,000-fold difference in stringency.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge chromium, including metal plating and finishing shops, stainless steel producers, leather tanneries, and wood preservative makers, would face pressure to control releases; water utilities in affected cities would pay for treatment to meet a stricter standard.

drawbacks.text: A stringent national standard would impose real treatment and compliance costs on water utilities, which could be passed to ratepayers, and on industrial dischargers; the bill set deadlines measured in months, faster than typical EPA rulemaking.
The bill directed the EPA to move notwithstanding normal Safe Drinking Water Act procedures, compressing the science review and public comment process that usually shapes drinking water standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is straightforward: Chrome 6 is classified as a known human carcinogen when inhaled, and EPA's own draft review found it likely carcinogenic in drinking water, yet the federal standard has not been updated since 1991. The costs fall on utilities and dischargers and would partly flow to ratepayers, but the bill's very short deadlines left little room for the usual scientific review; a more deliberate timeline could have reached a similar standard with less disruption. On balance the bill addressed a documented gap in tap water protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and the Economy subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on March 27, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and never received a hearing or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that use or discharge hexavalent chromium, such as chrome plating and metal finishing shops, stainless steel producers, and leather tanneries, and the water utilities that would have had to treat for the contaminant, are better off because no stricter standard was imposed; the roughly two-thirds of tested cities found to contain Chrome 6 remain under the 1991 standard.

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and supported its referral; it carried his findings on chromium contamination in 35 tested cities.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Fred Upton, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 30, 2012 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only cosponsors were two House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, so the bill never attracted the cross-party support typically needed to move through a committee then controlled by Republicans; no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.industry: Metal finishing, chrome plating, and stainless steel production
industries.note: These industries use Chrome 6 widely, and EPA-reported releases totaled nearly 8 million pounds of chromium in 2009; a strict water standard would have forced them to control discharges. Their interest in avoiding a new standard runs against the public's interest in cleaner tap water.

The bill's findings list both as users of Chrome 6; a stringent drinking water rule would raise their discharge-control obligations. Their cost-avoidance interest conflicts with the health protection the bill promised.

Utilities in cities with detected Chrome 6 would have had to install treatment to meet a standard far below the 1991 total-chromium limit, a cost likely passed to ratepayers; they also exist to deliver safe water, which the bill would advance.
